posts.title: How to Install Docker: The Complete Beginner Guide
posts.excerpt: Docker can feel intimidating at first. Here's how I install it, verify it works, and get from zero to running containers in under 10 minutes on any OS.

sections.content: The first time I heard about Docker I thought it was something only big companies used. Turns out it's one of the most useful tools a developer can have — on any project, any size, any team. This guide gets you from zero to running containers, no experience needed.
What Docker actually is

Docker lets you package an application and everything it needs to run — the code, the runtime, the libraries, the config — into a single unit called a container. That container runs the same way on your laptop, your colleague's machine, and your production server. No more "it works on my machine".
A container is not a virtual machine. It doesn't emulate hardware. It shares the host OS kernel and starts in milliseconds instead of minutes.
Install on Linux (Ubuntu / Debian)
The cleanest way to install Docker on Ubuntu or Debian is using the official convenience script. Open your terminal and run these commands one by one:

# Remove any old versions first
sudo apt remove docker docker-engine docker.io containerd runc

# Install dependencies
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg

# Add Docker's official GPG key
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg

# Add the Docker repository
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

# Install Docker Engine
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
After installing, add your user to the docker group so you don't need sudo every time:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
newgrp docker
Install on Mac and Windows
On Mac and Windows, install Docker Desktop — it gives you Docker Engine, Docker Compose, and a GUI dashboard in one package.

items: Go to docs.docker.com/get-docker and download the installer for your OS
Run the installer and follow the prompts
Launch Docker Desktop from your Applications folder
Wait for the whale icon in your taskbar/menu bar to stop animating — that means Docker is running

sections.content: Verify your install
Run this in your terminal to confirm everything is working:

docker --version
# Docker version 25.0.3, build 4debf41

docker compose version
# Docker Compose version v2.24.6
Run your first container
This is the moment it clicks. Run the official hello-world image:
docker run hello-world
Docker will pull the image from Docker Hub, create a container, run it, print a confirmation message, and stop. The whole thing takes about 5 seconds. You just ran your first container.
Next steps

Now that Docker is installed, the next posts in this series walk through setting up a Python app, a Node.js environment, and eventually deploying a container so anyone can use it. Docker gets more powerful the more you use it — the learning curve is front-loaded, and it pays off fast.

posts.title: How to Run Your Python App in a Docker Container
posts.excerpt: Stop installing Python versions and managing virtual environments per project. Here's how I containerize any Python app and run it exactly the same everywhere.

sections.content: Every Python developer has been there — spending 30 minutes debugging why an app works on one machine and not another because of a Python version mismatch or a missing package. Docker solves this permanently. Once you containerize your app, the environment is part of the code.
Why Docker for Python specifically

items: No more pyenv, virtualenv, or conda conflicts between projects
Your exact Python version and packages are locked in the image
New team members clone the repo and run one command — done
Identical environment from your laptop to the server

sections.content: Writing the Dockerfile
Create a file named Dockerfile in the root of your Python project. Here's a solid starting point that works for Flask, FastAPI, Django, or any script:

# Use an official slim Python image
FROM python:3.11-slim

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy requirements first (Docker caches this layer)
COPY requirements.txt .

# Install dependencies
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy the rest of your app
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app runs on
EXPOSE 8000

# Start the app
CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
For a Flask app, swap the last line to: CMD ["python", "-m", "flask", "run", "--host=0.0.0.0", "--port=8000"]. For a plain script: CMD ["python", "main.py"].
Adding Docker Compose
Create a docker-compose.yml file. This is how you actually run things — it's simpler than typing long docker run commands every time:

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    environment:
      - DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:15
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: pass
      POSTGRES_DB: mydb
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  pgdata:
Hot reload with volumes

Notice volumes: - .:/app in the compose file. This mounts your local project folder inside the container in real time. When you edit a file locally, the container sees the change immediately — so if you're using FastAPI with --reload or Flask with debug mode, you get hot reload without rebuilding the image.
Build and run

# Build the image and start all services
docker compose up --build

# Run in background (detached mode)
docker compose up -d --build

# Stop everything
docker compose down

# See logs
docker compose logs -f app

Your app is now running at http://localhost:8000 inside a fully isolated container. No virtual environment, no Python version drama, no missing packages. Just your app running exactly as it will in production.

posts.title: How to Set Up a Node.js Docker Environment
posts.excerpt: The exact Dockerfile and Compose setup I use for every Node.js project — with hot reload, environment variables, and a separate dev vs prod config.

sections.content: Node.js and Docker are a natural fit — Node apps are lightweight, fast to containerize, and behave consistently across environments. This is the exact setup I use as a starting point for every Node.js project, whether it's a REST API, an Express server, or a background worker.
Project structure

my-node-app/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── Dockerfile
├── Dockerfile.dev
├── docker-compose.yml
├── docker-compose.dev.yml
├── .dockerignore
├── package.json
└── .env
Always create a .dockerignore file to keep your image lean. At minimum it should contain:

node_modules
npm-debug.log
.env
.git
dist
The Dockerfile (production)

FROM node:20-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first (cache layer)
COPY package*.json .

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Copy source
COPY . .

# Expose port
EXPOSE 3000

# Start
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
Using node:20-alpine instead of node:20 cuts your image size from ~1GB down to ~180MB. Using npm ci instead of npm install ensures reproducible installs from the lockfile.
Dev Compose config with hot reload

# docker-compose.dev.yml
services:
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.dev
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      - .:/app
      - /app/node_modules
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=development
    env_file:
      - .env
    command: npm run dev

The trick with Node volumes is - /app/node_modules — this tells Docker to use the container's own node_modules folder rather than syncing yours from the host. Prevents conflicts between your local OS and the container OS.
Production Compose config

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file:
      - .env
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
Useful scripts to add to package.json

"scripts": {
  "dev":          "nodemon src/index.js",
  "docker:dev":   "docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build",
  "docker:prod":  "docker compose up --build -d",
  "docker:down":  "docker compose down",
  "docker:logs":  "docker compose logs -f app"
}
With this setup, npm run docker:dev spins up your full dev environment with hot reload in one command. Your colleagues clone the repo, run the same command, and everything works. That's the point.

posts.title: How to Deploy a Docker Container and Share It With Everyone
posts.excerpt: Building an image is step one. Getting it running on a server anyone can reach is the whole game. Here's exactly how I do it.

toc.label: Pull and run on the server

sections.content: You've built your app, it runs perfectly in Docker on your machine. Now what? This post walks through pushing your image to a registry and running it on a server so anyone with a browser can reach it — the complete path from local container to live URL.
Step 1 — Push your image to Docker Hub
Docker Hub is the default public registry — free for public images. First, create a free account at hub.docker.com, then:

# Login to Docker Hub
docker login

# Build and tag your image
docker build -t yourusername/myapp:latest .

# Push to the registry
docker push yourusername/myapp:latest

Your image is now publicly available. Anyone can pull it with docker pull yourusername/myapp. For private images, Docker Hub offers one free private repo, or you can use GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io) which is free for public repos.
Step 2 — Set up your VPS
Any VPS works — DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Linode, whatever. Get a Ubuntu 22.04 droplet (the cheapest one is fine for most apps), SSH in, and install Docker:

# SSH into your server
ssh root@your-server-ip

# Install Docker (same as before)
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh

# Add your user to docker group
usermod -aG docker $USER
Step 3 — Pull and run your container on the server

# Pull your image
docker pull yourusername/myapp:latest

# Run it — restart always means it survives reboots
docker run -d \
  --name myapp \
  --restart always \
  -p 3000:3000 \
  --env-file .env \
  yourusername/myapp:latest

# Check it's running
docker ps
docker logs myapp
Step 4 — Expose it with Nginx and a domain
Your app is running on port 3000 but you want it on a proper domain with HTTPS. Install Nginx as a reverse proxy:

sudo apt install -y nginx certbot python3-certbot-nginx

# Create a site config
sudo nano /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp

# Enable the site
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

# Add free HTTPS with Let's Encrypt
sudo certbot --nginx -d myapp.yourdomain.com
Step 5 — Deploying updates
Every time you want to ship a new version, the flow is:

# On your local machine
docker build -t yourusername/myapp:latest .
docker push yourusername/myapp:latest

# On the server
docker pull yourusername/myapp:latest
docker stop myapp && docker rm myapp
docker run -d --name myapp --restart always -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env yourusername/myapp:latest

That's it. Your app is live, has HTTPS, survives server reboots, and can be updated in under a minute. From here you can automate this deploy flow with a simple GitHub Actions workflow — push to main, image builds and deploys automatically.

posts.title: How to Design a Good API: 10 Steps I Actually Use
posts.excerpt: API design is one of those things that looks easy until you're six months in and everything is a mess. These are the 10 steps that keep me out of trouble.

sections.content: A bad API is one of the most expensive things a team can build. It's invisible until it isn't — and when it becomes a problem, it's usually deeply embedded in client code you don't control. These 10 steps are my checklist for every API I design, whether it's public-facing or internal.
1. Design for the consumer first

Start by asking: who calls this API and what do they need? Write the requests and responses you want the consumer to make before you write a single line of server code. This is called API-first design and it prevents the most common mistake — designing an API around your database schema instead of your consumer's needs.
2. Think in resources, not actions
REST APIs are built around nouns, not verbs. Your URLs should represent things, not operations.

items: Good: POST /invoices to create, GET /invoices/42 to fetch
Bad: POST /createInvoice, GET /getInvoiceById?id=42
Use HTTP methods (GET, POST, PATCH, DELETE) to express the operation — not the URL

sections.content: 3. Version from day one

Put a version in your base path from the very first endpoint: /api/v1/. It feels unnecessary until the day you need to make a breaking change and you're glad you did. Changing an API without versioning means breaking every client that uses it.
4. Use HTTP status codes correctly

items: 200 — success with a body
201 — resource created (use after POST)
204 — success with no body (use after DELETE)
400 — bad request (client's fault, fix your input)
401 — not authenticated (who are you?)
403 — not authorized (I know who you are, you can't do this)
404 — not found
409 — conflict (duplicate, version mismatch)
500 — server error (your fault, not the client's)

sections.content: 5. Pick one error shape and stick to it
Every error response in your API should look exactly the same. Clients shouldn't have to handle five different error formats. Pick a shape and enforce it everywhere:
6. Paginate every list endpoint

Never return an unbounded list. Every endpoint that returns a collection needs pagination from day one — you will never regret adding it early, and you will always regret not having it. Use cursor-based pagination for large datasets, offset-based for simple cases:
7. Support filtering, sorting, and search from the start

Build ?filter[status]=active, ?sort=-createdAt, and ?search=keyword into your list endpoints. Clients will always need these. Adding them later means deprecating old endpoints or breaking existing consumers.
8. Secure by default

items: Every endpoint should require authentication unless explicitly public
Use short-lived JWT access tokens + refresh token rotation
Rate limit every endpoint — even internal ones
Validate and sanitize every input, even fields you don't use
Never expose internal IDs — use UUIDs or slugs in URLs

sections.content: 9. Write the documentation before you build

Write your OpenAPI spec (or at minimum a README with example requests and responses) before you write the implementation. This forces you to think through the design first, catches ambiguities before they become bugs, and gives your team something to review and align on. I use this as a contract between me and whoever will consume the API.
10. Treat breaking changes like bugs

Removing a field, changing a field type, or altering a status code meaning are all breaking changes. Treat them with the same seriousness as a production bug. Add a deprecation warning in response headers before removing anything, give consumers a migration period, and never break the contract without a version bump. Your API is a promise.
A good API makes the right thing easy and the wrong thing hard. Everything else is details.

posts.title: How to Set Up and Install Kubernetes (k8s) Locally
posts.excerpt: Kubernetes looks terrifying until you run it yourself. Here's how I go from zero to a working local cluster using minikube — with a real app deployed on it.

sections.content: Kubernetes (k8s) has a reputation for being complicated. That reputation is partly deserved — it's a powerful system designed for large-scale production workloads. But you don't need a cluster of 50 nodes to learn it. Minikube runs a full Kubernetes cluster on your laptop, and once you've deployed one app yourself, the whole thing clicks into place.
What Kubernetes actually does

Docker runs a single container on a single machine. Kubernetes orchestrates many containers across many machines — automatically deciding where to run them, restarting them when they crash, scaling them up under load, and routing traffic between them. Think of it as Docker with a brain.
Kubernetes doesn't replace Docker. Every container in a Kubernetes cluster is still a Docker container. K8s is the system that manages and coordinates them.
Install minikube and kubectl
You need two tools: minikube (runs the local cluster) and kubectl (the CLI you use to talk to any cluster).

# Install kubectl (Linux)
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -L -s https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
sudo install -o root -g root -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl

# Install minikube (Linux)
curl -LO https://storage.googleapis.com/minikube/releases/latest/minikube-linux-amd64
sudo install minikube-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/minikube

# Verify both
kubectl version --client
minikube version
On Mac: brew install kubectl minikube. On Windows: use the installers from the official Kubernetes docs.
Start your first cluster

# Start a local cluster using Docker as the driver
minikube start --driver=docker

# Check it's running
kubectl get nodes
# NAME       STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
# minikube   Ready    control-plane   30s   v1.29.0

# Open the Kubernetes dashboard in your browser
minikube dashboard
Deploy a real app
Create a deployment.yml file — this tells Kubernetes what to run and how many copies to keep alive:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: myapp
        image: yourusername/myapp:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000

# Apply the deployment
kubectl apply -f deployment.yml

# Watch the pods come up
kubectl get pods -w
# NAME                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# myapp-7d6b9c8f4-xk2p9   1/1     Running   0          15s
# myapp-7d6b9c8f4-mn8qr   1/1     Running   0          15s
Expose it as a service

# Create a service to expose the deployment
kubectl expose deployment myapp --type=NodePort --port=3000

# Get the URL minikube assigns it
minikube service myapp --url
# http://192.168.49.2:31245  ← open this in your browser
Commands you'll actually use every day

kubectl get pods                    # list all running pods
kubectl get services                # list all services
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>     # debug a specific pod
kubectl logs <pod-name>             # see pod logs
kubectl logs -f <pod-name>          # stream logs live
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh   # shell into a running pod
kubectl delete -f deployment.yml    # tear everything down
minikube stop                       # stop the cluster
minikube delete                     # delete the cluster completely

From here the natural next steps are ConfigMaps and Secrets for environment variables, Ingress for routing multiple services through one domain, and Helm for packaging and deploying complex applications. But this foundation — deploy, expose, inspect — covers 80% of what you do day to day.

posts.title: How to Set Up ntfy for Free and Get Notified on Your Phone From Your PC
posts.excerpt: ntfy is a dead-simple self-hosted notification service. I use it to get alerts from servers, scripts, and backups straight to my phone — no paid service, no account required.

toc.label: Send a notification from your PC

sections.content: I run a lot of scripts and automated jobs — backups, deployments, monitoring checks. For the longest time I had no idea when they finished or failed unless I was watching the terminal. Then I found ntfy. Now my phone buzzes when a backup completes, when a deploy fails, or when a server is running low on disk. Setup took 10 minutes.
What ntfy is

ntfy (notify) is an open-source push notification service. You send an HTTP request to a topic URL, and everyone subscribed to that topic gets a notification. No accounts, no API keys, no SDK. Just a curl command. You can use the free public server at ntfy.sh or self-host your own.
Step 1 — Set up the phone app

items: Install the ntfy app from the App Store or Google Play — it's free and open source
Open the app and tap the + button to subscribe to a topic
Enter a topic name — make it something unique like mygildas-alerts (anyone who knows the name can send to it, so don't use something obvious)
Tap Subscribe — you're now listening for notifications on that topic

sections.content: Step 2 — Send your first notification from your PC
Open a terminal on your computer and run this one line:
curl -d "Backup completed successfully" ntfy.sh/mygildas-alerts
Your phone should buzz within a second. That's it. Now you can put that line anywhere — at the end of a backup script, after a deployment, in a cron job.
You can also add a title, priority, and emoji:

curl \
  -H "Title: Deploy Complete" \
  -H "Priority: high" \
  -H "Tags: white_check_mark" \
  -d "Production deployed successfully — v2.4.1" \
  ntfy.sh/mygildas-alerts
Step 3 — Self-host with Docker (optional but recommended)
The public ntfy.sh server is convenient but your topics are public by default. For private notifications, run your own server — it takes 2 minutes with Docker:

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  ntfy:
    image: binwiederhier/ntfy
    command: serve
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ntfy-cache:/var/cache/ntfy
      - ntfy-etc:/etc/ntfy
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  ntfy-cache:
  ntfy-etc:

docker compose up -d

# Now send to your own server
curl -d "Hello from self-hosted ntfy" http://localhost:8080/mygildas-alerts
In the ntfy phone app, go to Settings → Default server and point it at your server's IP or domain. Now all your topics are private.
Real use cases from my setup

items: Backup completion — restic backup /data && curl -d "Backup done" ntfy.sh/mytopic
Failed cron jobs — wrap any cron job in a script that sends a failure notification if the exit code isn't 0
Deployment status — last step in every CI/CD pipeline sends a pass or fail notification
Disk space warnings — a cron job that checks df -h every hour and notifies if any partition is over 85%
Script done — any long-running process: python train.py && curl -d "Training complete" ntfy.sh/mytopic

sections.content: ntfy is one of those tools where once you start using it you can't imagine going back. It takes the "I wonder if that finished" anxiety out of running long processes and background jobs. Free, open source, no accounts, no limits on self-hosted. Highly recommend.

posts.title: How to Run an LLM Locally With Ollama in a Docker Container
posts.excerpt: You don't need a cloud API to run a large language model. Here's how I run Llama, Mistral, and others locally using Ollama in Docker — private, free, and surprisingly fast.

sections.content: Running your own LLM locally used to require a PhD in MLOps. Ollama changed that. It's a tool that makes downloading and running open-source language models as simple as docker run and ollama pull llama3. Your data stays on your machine, there's no API bill, and the models are genuinely useful.
What Ollama is

Ollama is an open-source tool that packages LLM inference into a simple server with a REST API. It handles downloading model weights, loading them into memory, and serving a ChatGPT-style API on localhost. You interact with it exactly like you would the OpenAI API — just pointing at http://localhost:11434 instead.

Supported models include Llama 3, Mistral, Gemma, Phi-3, CodeLlama, and dozens more. For most tasks a 7B or 8B parameter model running on CPU is genuinely useful — code completion, summarization, Q&A, writing help.
Run Ollama in Docker
The easiest way to run Ollama is with Docker Compose. Create a docker-compose.yml:

services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama
    container_name: ollama
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
    volumes:
      - ollama-models:/root/.ollama
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  ollama-models:  # persists downloaded models between restarts

docker compose up -d

# Verify it's running
curl http://localhost:11434
# Ollama is running
Pull and run a model
Pull a model the same way you pull a Docker image:

# Pull Llama 3 (8B — ~4.7GB download)
docker exec -it ollama ollama pull llama3

# Pull Mistral (7B — ~4.1GB)
docker exec -it ollama ollama pull mistral

# Pull a smaller model for slower machines (Phi-3 mini — ~2.3GB)
docker exec -it ollama ollama pull phi3:mini

# List downloaded models
docker exec -it ollama ollama list

# Chat with a model directly in the terminal
docker exec -it ollama ollama run llama3
The first pull takes a few minutes depending on your connection. After that, the model is cached in the Docker volume and loads in seconds.
Use the REST API
Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 11434. You can call it with curl:

# Generate a response
curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate \
  -d '{
    "model":  "llama3",
    "prompt": "Explain Docker in one sentence.",
    "stream": false
  }'
Call it from Python
Because Ollama is OpenAI-compatible, you can use the official OpenAI Python library pointed at localhost — no API key needed:
pip install openai
This means any code you've written against the OpenAI API can switch to a local model by changing one URL and one API key. Useful for development and testing without burning API credits.
Enable GPU acceleration (optional)
If you have an NVIDIA GPU, you can make inference significantly faster by passing the GPU to the container. First install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, then update your compose file:

services:
  ollama:
    image: ollama/ollama
    ports:
      - "11434:11434"
    volumes:
      - ollama-models:/root/.ollama
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: all
              capabilities: [gpu]
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  ollama-models:

With a GPU, a 7B model goes from ~10 tokens/second on CPU to ~60-80 tokens/second — the difference between sluggish and genuinely fast. Even without a GPU though, the smaller models like Phi-3 mini are fast enough for real use on a modern laptop.
Running your own LLM means your data never leaves your machine. For anything involving sensitive code, client data, or private documents — that's not a nice-to-have, it's a requirement.
